newsitem.title: USA: RESEARCH ALERT - Merrill bullish on Micron Q1.
newsitem.headline: RESEARCH ALERT - Merrill bullish on Micron Q1.

text.p: -- Merrill Lynch analyst Tom Kurlak said Micron Technology Inc is poised to produce a substantial upside earnings surprise when it reports earnings for its current fiscal first quarter ending in November.

-- He said that his surveys of chipmakers and large memory chip customers has found that pricing on the spot market worldwide for the most popular type of computer memory chips has staged a dramatic turnaround in the last five weeks.
-- Kurlak said he is considering raising his estimate for the quarter from $0.25 per share. He said improved prices could push Micron earnings as high as $0.45 per share.
-- The consensus among analysts for Micron's first quarter is for the company to eke out a small profit of $0.01 per share, according to First Call.

-- Kurlak argued Micron is uniquely positioned to benefit because it sells most of its 16-meg memories in the spot market, as opposed to the contract market, where suppliers like Texas Instruments Inc sell most of their memory.

-- He said prices on the spot market for 16-meg Dynamic Random Access Memory DRAM chips have ranged between $11 and $14 per device in the last five weeks. By contrast, scheduled contract pricing has ranged between $8.50 and $10.50, he said.
-- "The market has reversed about 180 degrees in the past two months," Kurlak said, noting that spot pricing for 16-meg DRAMs were beneath $7 per device in July.

-- "All this extra money is going straight to the bottom line for Micron," he said. "We think there is an upside earnings surprise coming in the Novemember quarter and that this condition will be ongoing," the analyst said.

-- As a result, he said he was considering raising his earnings estimates for the current quarter and beyond. He also said this gives credibility to his fiscal 1997 year estimate of $1.95 a share, well ahead of the consensus of $0.71.

-- Kurlak said many of the world's leading memory chip makers are complaining of capacity constraints -- a startling switch from conditions over the last year, when a vast inventory oversupply caused a drastic fall in memory pricing.

-- While Wall Street remains concerned about excess factory capacity, Kurlak refered to this as "the past year's problem." The opposite is true, he argued, now that capital spending for chip factories has slowed and demand has caught supply. Memory chip production backlogs are once again occuring, he believes.

-- He said his aggressive view was based on talks with some of the world's top DRAM makers, such as Hitachi Ltd, NEC Corp and Micron and big memory customers, like Compaq Computer Corp and Hewlett-Packard Co.
